headline: Illinois hemp sellers lose bid to block Hemp Act on 19 November
dek: A federal judge in Chicago denied a restraining order against the Illinois Hemp Act, ending a pause that covered about 250 hemp businesses.
key_points: U.S. District Judge Martha Pacold denied the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association's request for a temporary restraining order on 19 November, without prejudice.
The state's agreement not to enforce the law against the plaintiffs and association members was due to expire at 5 p.m. the same day.
The lawsuit continues: the group will pursue a preliminary injunction and says it is exploring an appeal.
In Washington, Senators Ted Budd and Pete Ricketts said they will oppose any funding bill that delays or replaces the federal hemp ban due on 11 December.
body: Illinois' hemp industry has lost the first round in federal court. On Thursday 19 November, U.S. District Judge Martha Pacold of the Northern District of Illinois denied an emergency request to temporarily block the Illinois Hemp Act, The Marijuana Herald reported. The request came from the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association (ILHAA), a trade group, and five hemp businesses.

The denial was without prejudice, which means the plaintiffs can ask again, and it does not decide whether the law is constitutional. But it removes the protection that about 250 businesses have had since the law took effect on 12 November. As we reported on 10 November, Illinois had agreed not to enforce the new rules against the plaintiffs and qualifying ILHAA members until the hearing. That agreement was set to end at 5 p.m. on 19 November, according to the Herald.
## What the judge decided, and what she did not

A temporary restraining order is the fastest form of court relief: a short freeze granted when a party shows it will suffer serious harm before the court can hear the case properly. Judge Pacold declined to grant one after the hearing. The plaintiffs' separate request for a preliminary injunction, a longer pause that lasts while the case is argued, is still open, as is the lawsuit itself.

ILHAA's Craig Katz said the group disagrees with the decision, will press its claims at the preliminary injunction stage and is "exploring review in the appellate court", according to the Herald. The Herald's report does not set out the judge's reasoning, and we have not seen a written order.

The lawsuit was filed on 5 November. It argues that the Illinois law violates the Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which limits how far a state can burden trade between states, and that it threatens heavy economic harm. ILHAA says its roughly 250 member companies employ more than 5,000 people in Illinois, including farmers, processors, manufacturers, distributors and retailers.
## What the Illinois law does

The Illinois Hemp Act was part of legislation Governor JB Pritzker signed in June. It treats hemp-derived products with more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container as cannabis, so they can be sold only by licensed cannabis dispensaries. That covers products made with delta-8 THC, delta-9 THC and THCA. Hemp products under the limit, including many CBD products, can still be sold in ordinary shops if they meet testing, packaging and labelling rules, the Herald reported.

The 0.4 milligram figure mirrors the federal cap Congress wrote into law in November 2025. Congress later pushed the federal effective date for most products to 11 December 2026. Illinois did not move its own date, so the state limit has applied since 12 November, four weeks ahead of the federal one. As we reported on 13 November, state regulators can fine sellers up to $10,000 per offence, with each day of sales counted separately.
> For Illinois hemp sellers the legal question is still open, but the commercial one is not: from today the shelf rules apply to everyone.
## What changes for sellers now

Until Thursday, Illinois had two classes of hemp seller: ILHAA members and the named plaintiffs, who were shielded by the state's agreement, and everyone else, who had to comply from 12 November. With the restraining order denied and the agreement at its end, that distinction falls away unless the state and the plaintiffs agree a new pause or a court orders one. Neither had been reported at the time of writing.

In practice, a shop, bar or liquor store that kept selling THC drinks or gummies over the limit under the pause now faces the same exposure as any other seller. Licensed cannabis dispensaries are the only lawful outlet for those products in the state. Businesses that held stock in the hope of a court win will have to decide whether to keep holding it until the injunction ruling or to clear it.
## Washington: two senators draw a line

The Illinois ruling lands as the federal fight hardens. On 17 November, Senators Tim Sheehy and Amy Klobuchar introduced the Hemp Guardrails Act, which would replace the 11 December ban with federal product rules, as we reported on 18 November. The same day, Sen. Ted Budd of North Carolina said in a social media post that he will not support any year-end package that extends, delays or builds a regulatory framework around these products, The Hype Magazine reported, citing Marijuana Moment. Budd said Congress closed the hemp loophole to end "an industry that never should have existed".

Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska said he agreed and would not support legislation that lets the products stay on sale, according to the same report. When we covered the Sheehy-Klobuchar bill we flagged that Budd and Ricketts could tie hemp to their votes on the funding bill. Both have now said so in public.

Their position matters because of how supporters plan to move. Rep. James Comer has said a continuing resolution is the one bill that has to pass, and the U.S. Hemp Roundtable has said it wants the Guardrails Act's provisions in the next spending bill. Two senators cannot block a funding bill alone. But in a short lame-duck session, leaders tend to avoid provisions that cost votes, so public opposition raises the price of adding hemp language. That reading is ours.
## What it means

Illinois now shows what the federal ban would look like if it arrives on schedule: products over 0.4 milligrams per container move into licensed cannabis stores or leave the market, and a court challenge on constitutional grounds does not, at least at the emergency stage, stop the clock. Operators in other states that copied the federal cap should not count on quick relief from a federal court. That is an inference from one ruling, and other judges may see other laws differently.

For licensed Illinois dispensaries, the ruling keeps the rerouting of hemp-derived THC sales into their channel in place. For drinks makers and retailers outside the cannabis system, the next 21 days decide whether there is a federal market to sell into at all.
## What to watch

Watch for a schedule for the preliminary injunction in the Illinois case and for any appeal to the Seventh Circuit. Watch whether Illinois regulators begin enforcement against businesses that were covered by the pause. In Congress, watch the text of the next funding bill for any hemp delay or the Guardrails Act's language, and the vote counts if Budd and Ricketts hold their position. The federal cap takes effect on 11 December unless Congress acts.
